request.project_context: pygame 双人乒乓球 采用 Python + pygame 单文件结构：pygame.time.Clock 与 dt（秒）驱动移动，速度以“像素/秒”表示，位置累加 v*dt。键盘处理区分两类输入：出界得分流程中用事件队列里的 KEYDOWN 捕获空格发球与 R 重开；移动用 pygame.key.get_pressed() 读取按住状态并配合坐标夹取把球拍限制在屏内。碰撞用矩形碰撞与球速分量取反（碰上下边界取反 vy，碰球拍取反 vx 并按需修正位置避免重复触发）。比分与状态用简单状态字段（如 playing/paused_by_score/over）加分数列表驱动，暂停期间仍绘制并继续处理事件与退出，重开时重置分数、球位置与速度。所有逻辑在同一个主循环内，Esc 与 QUIT 在任何状态都被处理。 会 Python 函数/列表和 pygame 窗口、绘图、离散按键事件；未做持续输入、速度运动、反弹和一局多轮状态。 用 pygame 做本地双人乒乓球。W/S控制左拍、上下键控制右拍，按住可持续移动且球拍不出屏；球按经过时间移动，碰上下边界或球拍反弹。出左右边界给另一方加1分，显示比分并暂停等空格发球，先到3分显示获胜；获胜后R重开，Esc/关窗始终可退出。固定单屏，不做AI、联网、音效或物理引擎。

resources.description: import pygame import random import time pygame.init() # 游戏窗口 window_width = 800 window_height = 600 # 颜色 black = (0, 0, 0) white = (255, 255, 255) # 创建 window = pygame.display.set_mode((window_width, window_height)) pygame.display.set_caption("躲躲躲1.0") # 游戏时钟 clock = pygame.time.Clock() # 玩家 player_radius = 20 player_x = window_width // 2 player_y = window_height - player_radius player_speed = 10 # 障碍物 obstacle_width = 100 obstacle_height = 20 obstacle_x = random.randint(0, window_width - obstacle_width) obstacle_y = 0 obstacle_speed = 3 # 游戏难度 difficulty = 1 # 游戏结束 game_over = False # 存活时间 start_time = time.time() # 游戏循环 while not game_over: for event in pygame.event.get(): if event.type == pygame.QUIT: game_over = True # 键盘输入 keys = pygame.key.get_pressed() if keys[pygame.K_LEFT]: player_x -= player_speed if keys[pygame.K_RIGHT]: player_x += player_speed # 更新玩家 if player_x < 0: player_x = 0 elif player_x > window_width - player_radius: player_x = window_width - player_radius # 更新障碍物 obstacle_y += obstacle_speed * difficulty # 检测碰撞 if obstacle_y > window_height: obstacle_x = random.randint(0, window_width - obstacle_width) obstacle_y = 0 difficulty += 0.1 if (obstacle_y <= player_y + player_radius <= obstacle_y + obstacle_height) and ( obstacle_x <= player_x <= obstacle_x + obstacle_width): game_over = True # 绘制游戏场景 window.fill(black) pygame.draw.circle(window, white, (player_x, player_y), player_radius) pygame.draw.rect(window, white, (obstacle_x, obstacle_y, obstacle_width, obstacle_height)) pygame.display.update() # 控制游戏帧率 clock.tick(60) # 计算存活时间 end_time = time.time() survival_time = int(end_time - start_time) # 输出存活时间 print("存活时间：", survival_time, "秒") # 游戏结束，退出Pygame pygame.quit()

resources.description:
Projectiles
In this tutorial we are going to be implementing projectiles.
Projectile Class
The first thing we are going to do is create a projectile class.
Modifying the Player Class
Because we are going to be shooting bullets left or right we need to ensure our character is always facing left or right. This required modifying the player.draw method and adding another attribute of standing to our player.
Modifying the Main Loop
We also need to modify our main loop to ensure our character is always facing left or right.
Setting up The Projectiles
The first step is to create a list which will store all of our bullet objects.
bullets = [] # This goes right above the while loop
Now we are going to add a for loop into our main loop that will move our bullets and remove them if they have left the screen.
# Goes inside the while loop for bullet in bullets: if bullet.x < 500 and bullet.x > 0: bullet.x += bullet.vel # Moves the bullet by its vel else: bullets.pop(bullets.index(bullet)) # This will remove the bullet if it is off the screen
Shooting the Bullet
We are first going to change our jump key to be the up arrow (just change pygame.K_SPACE to pygame.K_UP). Then we are going to create a new if statement that will check if the space bar is clicked. If it is we will create a new bullet, give it a velocity and start moving it.
And the last thing to do is to draw our bullets inside redrawGameWindow().
```python
def redrawGameWindow():
    win.blit(bg, (0,0))
    man.draw(win)
    for bullet in bullets:
        bullet.draw(win)

    pygame.display.update()
```
Now we can fire bullets!

# This goes outside the while loop, near the top of our program left = False right = False walkCount = 0

resources.description:
Collision & Hit Boxes
In many games we need to check for different types of collision. Whether that be collision of our mouse with a button or collision between images and/or objects. In our case we want to check if our goblin has hit the player or if our bullets have hit the goblin.
Hit Boxes
The term "hit box" is often used to represent the box around an object which represents its "hittable space". Since we often use complex objects and shapes to depict characters or other items in a game we create a hit box for all of these items. This makes it much easier to check for collision as collision between non-rectangular shapes is extremely complicated. We attempt to make these boxes fit the characters shape as precisely as possible but it is difficult to make them perfect.
We will start by creating hit boxes for all of our objects. Then we check if these boxes collide with one another using some basic math.
The first hit box we define will be for our player class.

resources.description:
Basic Movement & Key Presses
What is Pygame?
Pygame is a third party module designed for creating 2D games with python. It has very simple and intuitive syntax that can allows us to create powerful games quickly. Pygame uses surfaces for drawing. This means whenever we want to draw something to the screen it must be converted to a surface. There are many methods and functions within pygame that can do this easily for us.
Installing Pygame
Installing pygame can be as easy as:
Opening your command prompt Typing pip install pygame
However, in many cases this will not work. Below are guides for installing pygame on both windows and mac.
Windows: How to Install Pygame on Windows
Mac OS: How to Install Pygame on Mac
Linux: refer to the Mac OS Guide.
Creating a Window
After we import pygame it is a good idea to initialize it, like so:
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()
```
Once we've done that we need to setup a windows that will represent our game.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500, 500))
# This line creates a window of 500 width, 500 height
```
Now when we run the program we get something that looks like this.
This is great but we'd like to give our game a more creative name than "pygame window". To do this we can can type the following.
```python
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")
```
That's better!
Moving a Character
We are going to start by defining a few variables to represent our character.
x = 50 y = 50 width = 40 height = 60 vel = 5
Now we are going to setup our Main-loop or game-loop. All games have some sort of loop that executes constantly. This loop is responsible for tasks such as checking for events (such as keyboard events or collision), moving objects, updating the display and eventually ending the game. In our game we will use a while loop.
Inside the loop we will implement a time delay so we can control the speed of the game. We will also start by checking for some specific events.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100) # This will delay the game the given amount of milliseconds. In our casee 0.1 seconds will be the delay

    for event in pygame.event.get():  # This will loop through a list of any keyboard or mouse events.
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT: # Checks if the red button in the corner of the window is clicked
            run = False  # Ends the game loop

pygame.quit()  # If we exit the loop this will execute and close our game
```
Now we can draw a rectangle to the screen to represent our character. We will draw the rectangle in the main loop so that it is constantly redrawn each time we loop.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100)

    for event in pygame.event.get():
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
            run = False

    pygame.draw.rect(win, (255,0,0), (x, y, width, height))  #This takes: window/surface, color, rect 
    pygame.display.update() # This updates the screen so we can see our rectangle

pygame.quit()
```
Now we can start checking for events so that we can move our character.
Inside the if statements we will change the value of the variables x and y to move the character. This brings me to the coordinate system. In pygame the top left corner of the screen is (0,0) and the bottom right is (width, height). This means to move up we subtract from the y of our character and to move down we add to the y.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100)

    for event in pygame.event.get():
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
            run = False

    keys = pygame.key.get_pressed()

    if keys[pygame.K_LEFT]:
        x -= vel

    if keys[pygame.K_RIGHT]:
        x += vel

    if keys[pygame.K_UP]:
        y -= vel

    if keys[pygame.K_DOWN]:
        y += vel

    pygame.draw.rect(win, (255,0,0), (x, y, width, height))   
    pygame.display.update() 

pygame.quit()
```
Now when we run the program and start moving our rectangle we can still see all of the previous rectangles.
To fix this we simply have to draw over the previous shape before redrawing another one. We can use window.fill(color) to do this.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100)

    for event in pygame.event.get():
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
            run = False

    keys = pygame.key.get_pressed()

    if keys[pygame.K_LEFT]:
        x -= vel

    if keys[pygame.K_RIGHT]:
        x += vel

    if keys[pygame.K_UP]:
        y -= vel

    if keys[pygame.K_DOWN]:
        y += vel

    win.fill((0,0,0))  # Fills the screen with black
    pygame.draw.rect(win, (255,0,0), (x, y, width, height))   
    pygame.display.update() 

pygame.quit()
```
And now we can move our character around!

resources.description:
Tutorial #1
In this tutorial series we will be working to create the famous snake game in python with the module pygame. If you are more interested in a general pygame tutorial series click here
Starter Code
To make our lives a bit easier I've set up the main structure for our game already. We are going to be using two main classes (snake and cube).
Creating our Game Loop
In all games we have a loop called a "main loop" or "game loop". This loop will continuously run until the game is exited. It is mainly responsible for checking for events and calling functions and methods based on those events.
We are going to be coding our game loop inside the main() function. We will declare some variables at the top of the function then move into our while loop which will represent our game loop.
```python
def main(): 
    global width, rows, s
    width = 500  # Width of our screen
    height = 500  # Height of our screen
    rows = 20  # Amount of rows

    win = pygame.display.set_mode((width, height))  # Creates our screen object

    s = snake((255,0,0), (10,10))  # Creates a snake object which we will code later

    clock = pygame.time.Clock() # creating a clock object

    flag = True
    # STARTING MAIN LOOP
    while flag:
        pygame.time.delay(50)  # This will delay the game so it doesn't run too quickly
        clock.tick(10)  # Will ensure our game runs at 10 FPS
        redrawWindow(win)  # This will refresh our screen
```
Updating the Screen
It is usually good practice to do all of our drawing of objects from within one function or method. We will be using the redrawWindow function to update the display. We call this function once a frame from our game loop.
We will be adding more to this function later. However, for now we will simply draw the grid lines.
Drawing the Grid
We are now going to work on drawing the lines to represent the 20x20 grid. We will do this in the drawGrid function.
```python
def drawGrid(w, rows, surface):
    sizeBtwn = w // rows  # Gives us the distance between the lines

    x = 0  # Keeps track of the current x
    y = 0  # Keeps track of the current y
    for l in range(rows):  # We will draw one vertical and one horizontal line each loop
        x = x + sizeBtwn
        y = y + sizeBtwn

        pygame.draw.line(surface, (255,255,255), (x,0),(x,w))
        pygame.draw.line(surface, (255,255,255), (0,y),(w,y))
```
Now when we run the program we can see the grid lines being drawn.
Starting the Snake Class
Our snake object is going to contain a list of cubes which will represent the snake body. We are going to store these cubes in a list called body which will be a class variable. We will also have a class variable called turns.
To start our Snake class we will code the init() method and add the class variables.

```

It is usually good practice to do all of our drawing of objects from within one function or method. We will be using the redrawWindow function to update the display. We call this function once a frame from our game loop.
We will be adding more to this function later. However, for now we will simply draw the grid lines.
Drawing the Grid
We are now going to work on drawing the lines to represent the 20x20 grid. We will do this in the drawGrid function.
```python
def drawGrid(w, rows, surface):
    sizeBtwn = w // rows  # Gives us the distance between the lines

    x = 0  # Keeps track of the current x
    y = 0  # Keeps track of the current y
    for l in range(rows):  # We will draw one vertical and one horizontal line each loop
        x = x + sizeBtwn
        y = y + sizeBtwn

        pygame.draw.line(surface, (255,255,255), (x,0),(x,w))
        pygame.draw.line(surface, (255,255,255), (0,y),(w,y))
```
Now when we run the program we can see the grid lines being drawn.
Starting the Snake Class
Our snake object is going to contain a list of cubes which will represent the snake body. We are going to store these cubes in a list called body which will be a class variable. We will also have a class variable called turns.
To start our Snake class we will code the init() method and add the class variables.

Tutorial #1
Starter File
To make our lives a little easier I have I have included a starter file that has the code for some of the more tedious parts of the game. Please copy the code below into your python script before starting. If you'd like an in-depth explanation of the starter file please refer to the video.
The way we will represent our pieces will be using multidimensional lists. Each list will have multiple sub-lists that represent all of the possible rotations of each shape. This will make it much easier to rotate and represent our shapes visually when we eventually draw them to the screen.
Piece Class
Since we will be creating multiple shapes it makes sense to create a piece class that can store some information about each shape.
Creating a Grid
The way that we will keep track of pieces in the game is using a grid data structure. We will create a multidimensional list that contains 20 lists of 10 elements (rows and columns). Each element in the lists will be a tuple representing the color of the piece in that current position. This will allow us to draw all of the colored squares quite easily as we can simply loop through the multidimensional list.
The locked position parameter will contain a dictionary of key value pairs where each key is a position of a piece that has already fallen and each value is its color. We will loop through these locked positions and modify our blank grid to show these pieces.
Getting a Random Shape
Since we will be dropping shapes down the screen at random we need to generate a random shape. This will be done in the get_shape() function.
Drawing the Grid
I am not going to explain all of the pygame functions and methods I use as if you are familair with pygame you should know them. However, if you'd like to learn more about the basics of pygame click here!
We will simply be calling the function below to draw all of our objects to the screen. In this function we call some functions that we will be coding later.
The Game Loop
In every game we have something called a game loop or a main loop. This is what will be running constantly and checking to see if events occur. Our game loop will go inside the main() function.
In this function we will start by defining some variables and then move into the while loop. Inside the while loop we will check for key press events and see if the user wants to exit the game.
When the user presses the up arrow key the piece will rotate. We can do this by simply increasing our shapes rotation attribute to be the next shape in the list we set up at the beginning of the program.
When the user hits the left or right arrow keys we will move accordingly bu changing the x value of our piece.
Finally when the user hist the down arrow key we will move down one square allowing the user to increase the speed at which the shape falls.
We will be adding more to this function in the future.
Setting up The Window
The last thing we need to do for this tutorial is setup the pygame window and give it a caption. This will go at the very end of the program, not within any function.
win = pygame.display.set_mode((s_width, s_height)) pygame.display.set_caption(\'Tetris\')
Testing The Program
If you'd like to test the program you can simply call main() at the very end of the program like so.
main()

Collision & Hit Boxes
In many games we need to check for different types of collision. Whether that be collision of our mouse with a button or collision between images and/or objects. In our case we want to check if our goblin has hit the player or if our bullets have hit the goblin.
Hit Boxes
The term "hit box" is often used to represent the box around an object which represents its "hittable space". Since we often use complex objects and shapes to depict characters or other items in a game we create a hit box for all of these items. This makes it much easier to check for collision as collision between non-rectangular shapes is extremely complicated. We attempt to make these boxes fit the characters shape as precisely as possible but it is difficult to make them perfect.
We will start by creating hit boxes for all of our objects. Then we check if these boxes collide with one another using some basic math.

In this tutorial we are going to be implementing projectiles.
Projectile Class
The first thing we are going to do is create a projectile class.
Modifying the Player Class
Because we are going to be shooting bullets left or right we need to ensure our character is always facing left or right. This required modifying the player.draw method and adding another attribute of standing to our player.
Modifying the Main Loop
We also need to modify our main loop to ensure our character is always facing left or right.
Setting up The Projectiles
The first step is to create a list which will store all of our bullet objects.
bullets = [] # This goes right above the while loop
Now we are going to add a for loop into our main loop that will move our bullets and remove them if they have left the screen.
# Goes inside the while loop for bullet in bullets: if bullet.x < 500 and bullet.x > 0: bullet.x += bullet.vel # Moves the bullet by its vel else: bullets.pop(bullets.index(bullet)) # This will remove the bullet if it is off the screen
Shooting the Bullet
We are first going to change our jump key to be the up arrow (just change pygame.K_SPACE to pygame.K_UP). Then we are going to create a new if statement that will check if the space bar is clicked. If it is we will create a new bullet, give it a velocity and start moving it.
And the last thing to do is to draw our bullets inside redrawGameWindow().
```python
def redrawGameWindow():
    win.blit(bg, (0,0))
    man.draw(win)
    for bullet in bullets:
        bullet.draw(win)

    pygame.display.update()
```
Now we can fire bullets!

Basic Movement & Key Presses
What is Pygame?
Pygame is a third party module designed for creating 2D games with python. It has very simple and intuitive syntax that can allows us to create powerful games quickly. Pygame uses surfaces for drawing. This means whenever we want to draw something to the screen it must be converted to a surface. There are many methods and functions within pygame that can do this easily for us.
Installing Pygame
Installing pygame can be as easy as:
Opening your command prompt Typing pip install pygame
However, in many cases this will not work. Below are guides for installing pygame on both windows and mac.
Windows: How to Install Pygame on Windows
Mac OS: How to Install Pygame on Mac
Linux: refer to the Mac OS Guide.
Creating a Window
After we import pygame it is a good idea to initialize it, like so:
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()
```
Once we've done that we need to setup a windows that will represent our game.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500, 500))
# This line creates a window of 500 width, 500 height
```
Now when we run the program we get something that looks like this.
This is great but we'd like to give our game a more creative name than "pygame window". To do this we can can type the following.
```python
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")
```
That's better!
Moving a Character
We are going to start by defining a few variables to represent our character.
x = 50 y = 50 width = 40 height = 60 vel = 5
Now we are going to setup our Main-loop or game-loop. All games have some sort of loop that executes constantly. This loop is responsible for tasks such as checking for events (such as keyboard events or collision), moving objects, updating the display and eventually ending the game. In our game we will use a while loop.
Inside the loop we will implement a time delay so we can control the speed of the game. We will also start by checking for some specific events.
```python

Basic Movement & Key Presses
What is Pygame?
Pygame is a third party module designed for creating 2D games with python. It has very simple and intuitive syntax that can allows us to create powerful games quickly. Pygame uses surfaces for drawing. This means whenever we want to draw something to the screen it must be converted to a surface. There are many methods and functions within pygame that can do this easily for us.
Installing Pygame
Installing pygame can be as easy as:
Opening your command prompt Typing pip install pygame
However, in many cases this will not work. Below are guides for installing pygame on both windows and mac.
Windows: How to Install Pygame on Windows
Mac OS: How to Install Pygame on Mac
Linux: refer to the Mac OS Guide.
Creating a Window
After we import pygame it is a good idea to initialize it, like so:
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()
```
Once we've done that we need to setup a windows that will represent our game.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500, 500))
# This line creates a window of 500 width, 500 height
```
Now when we run the program we get something that looks like this.
This is great but we'd like to give our game a more creative name than "pygame window". To do this we can can type the following.
```python
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")
```
That's better!
Moving a Character
We are going to start by defining a few variables to represent our character.
x = 50 y = 50 width = 40 height = 60 vel = 5
Now we are going to setup our Main-loop or game-loop. All games have some sort of loop that executes constantly. This loop is responsible for tasks such as checking for events (such as keyboard events or collision), moving objects, updating the display and eventually ending the game. In our game we will use a while loop.
Inside the loop we will implement a time delay so we can control the speed of the game. We will also start by checking for some specific events.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100) # This will delay the game the given amount of milliseconds. In our casee 0.1 seconds will be the delay

    for event in pygame.event.get():  # This will loop through a list of any keyboard or mouse events.
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT: # Checks if the red button in the corner of the window is clicked
            run = False  # Ends the game loop

pygame.quit()  # If we exit the loop this will execute and close our game
```
Now we can draw a rectangle to the screen to represent our character. We will draw the rectangle in the main loop so that it is constantly redrawn each time we loop.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100)

    for event in pygame.event.get():
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
            run = False

    pygame.draw.rect(win, (255,0,0), (x, y, width, height))  #This takes: window/surface, color, rect 
    pygame.display.update() # This updates the screen so we can see our rectangle

pygame.quit()
```
Now we can start checking for events so that we can move our character.
Inside the if statements we will change the value of the variables x and y to move the character. This brings me to the coordinate system. In pygame the top left corner of the screen is (0,0) and the bottom right is (width, height). This means to move up we subtract from the y of our character and to move down we add to the y.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100)

    for event in pygame.event.get():
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
            run = False

    keys = pygame.key.get_pressed()

    if keys[pygame.K_LEFT]:
        x -= vel

    if keys[pygame.K_RIGHT]:
        x += vel

    if keys[pygame.K_UP]:
        y -= vel

    if keys[pygame.K_DOWN]:
        y += vel

    pygame.draw.rect(win, (255,0,0), (x, y, width, height))   
    pygame.display.update() 

pygame.quit()
```
Now when we run the program and start moving our rectangle we can still see all of the previous rectangles.
To fix this we simply have to draw over the previous shape before redrawing another one. We can use window.fill(color) to do this.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100)

    for event in pygame.event.get():
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
            run = False

    keys = pygame.key.get_pressed()

    if keys[pygame.K_LEFT]:
        x -= vel

    if keys[pygame.K_RIGHT]:
        x += vel

    if keys[pygame.K_UP]:
        y -= vel

    if keys[pygame.K_DOWN]:
        y += vel

    win.fill((0,0,0))  # Fills the screen with black
    pygame.draw.rect(win, (255,0,0), (x, y, width, height))   
    pygame.display.update() 

pygame.quit()
```
And now we can move our character around!

Images

Note: The folder you downloaded has the images and assets for the entire finished game. The images that we will be working with in this tutorial end in an E.png
Loading Images
The following lists will be used a class variables to store our images for the enemy. We will place these lists inside of a class that we create in the next step.

walkRight = [pygame.image.load('R1E.png'), pygame.image.load('R2E.png'), pygame.image.load('R3E.png'), pygame.image.load('R4E.png'), pygame.image.load('R5E.png'), pygame.image.load('R6E.png'), pygame.image.load('R7E.png'), pygame.image.load('R8E.png'), pygame.image.load('R9E.png'), pygame.image.load('R10E.png'), pygame.image.load('R11E.png')]

Enemy Class
Like we've done in the previous tutorials we will use a class to create our enemy. We will start by pasting the code from above into our class. Then we will create the init method and set up some basic attributes for our enemy.
The next method we will add will be the draw() method. This will work similarly to our player classes draw method as we will also be doing animation in here.
The next method we add will be the move() method. This will move our enemy every frame. Since we want our enemy to be moving along a path we must figure out how much to move the enemy by and in what direction. We call this move method from our draw class as every time we draw the enemy we want to move first move it to a new position.
Creating an Enemy

Character Animation & Sprites
IMPORTANT Please download the images for this tutorial from my GitHub or the download button below.
GitHub: Click Here!
Download Zip:
Please place all of these images in the same directory as your python script.
Character Animation
After we've downloaded our images we can start getting ready to anime our character.
The first step is to create a few variables which will be used to determine which way we are facing and keep track of the current image we are showing.
# This goes outside the while loop, near the top of our program left = False right = False walkCount = 0
Now we need to load our images. To load an image in pygame we use pygame.image.load(path). Since we need to load so many images we will be storing some of them in lists for easier accessing later on.
This is the code to load all of our images (I recommend you copy and paste).
It is often good practice to do all of our drawing from within a function. This means we are going to move our old drawing code that is inside the main loop into a function and make a few modifications.
Now we are going to set our left and right variables appropriately from inside the main loop.
And finally we can start working on drawing our character to the screen.
NOTE: This is very complex, please refer to the video for more in depth explanations.
The last thing we need to do is change our framerate.
To do this we are going to create a clock object using clock = pygame.time.Clock() outside of our main loop and write clock.tick(27) inside our main loop.
You may notice when running the program that the background does not cover the entire screen, to fix this simply change there screen height to 480.
pygame.display.set_mode((500, 480))

import pygame import random import time pygame.init() # 游戏窗口 window_width = 800 window_height = 600 # 颜色 black = (0, 0, 0) white = (255, 255, 255) # 创建 window = pygame.display.set_mode((window_width, window_height)) pygame.display.set_caption("躲躲躲1.0") # 游戏时钟 clock = pygame.time.Clock() # 玩家 player_radius = 20 player_x = window_width // 2 player_y = window_height - player_radius player_speed = 10 # 障碍物 obstacle_width = 100 obstacle_height = 20 obstacle_x = random.randint(0, window_width - obstacle_width) obstacle_y = 0 obstacle_speed = 3 # 游戏难度 difficulty = 1 # 游戏结束 game_over = False # 存活时间 start_time = time.time() # 游戏循环 while not game_over: for event in pygame.event.get(): if event.type == pygame.QUIT: game_over = True # 键盘输入 keys = pygame.key.get_pressed() if keys[pygame.K_LEFT]: player_x -= player_speed if keys[pygame.K_RIGHT]: player_x += player_speed # 更新玩家 if player_x < 0: player_x = 0 elif player_x > window_width - player_radius: player_x = window_width - player_radius # 更新障碍物 obstacle_y += obstacle_speed * difficulty # 检测碰撞 if obstacle_y > window_height: obstacle_x = random.randint(0, window_width - obstacle_width) obstacle_y = 0 difficulty += 0.1 if (obstacle_y <= player_y + player_radius <= obstacle_y + obstacle_height) and ( obstacle_x <= player_x <= obstacle_x + obstacle_width): game_over = True # 绘制游戏场景 window.fill(black) pygame.draw.circle(window, white, (player_x, player_y), player_radius) pygame.draw.rect(window, white, (obstacle_x, obstacle_y, obstacle_width, obstacle_height)) pygame.display.update() # 控制游戏帧率 clock.tick(60) # 计算存活时间 end_time = time.time() survival_time = int(end_time - start_time) # 输出存活时间 print("存活时间：", survival_time, "秒") # 游戏结束，退出Pygame pygame.quit()

request.project_context: pygame 双人乒乓球 采用 Python + pygame 单文件结构：pygame.time.Clock 与 dt（秒）驱动移动，速度以“像素/秒”表示，位置累加 v*dt。键盘处理区分两类输入：出界得分流程中用事件队列里的 KEYDOWN 捕获空格发球与 R 重开；移动用 pygame.key.get_pressed() 读取按住状态并配合坐标夹取把球拍限制在屏内。碰撞用矩形碰撞与球速分量取反（碰上下边界取反 vy，碰球拍取反 vx 并按需修正位置避免重复触发）。比分与状态用简单状态字段（如 playing/paused_by_score/over）加分数列表驱动，暂停期间仍绘制并继续处理事件与退出，重开时重置分数、球位置与速度。所有逻辑在同一个主循环内，Esc 与 QUIT 在任何状态都被处理。 会 Python 函数/列表和 pygame 窗口、绘图、离散按键事件；未做持续输入、速度运动、反弹和一局多轮状态。 用 pygame 做本地双人乒乓球。W/S控制左拍、上下键控制右拍，按住可持续移动且球拍不出屏；球按经过时间移动，碰上下边界或球拍反弹。出左右边界给另一方加1分，显示比分并暂停等空格发球，先到3分显示获胜；获胜后R重开，Esc/关窗始终可退出。固定单屏，不做AI、联网、音效或物理引擎。

resources.description: 一个随机的 Timer 可以让 NPC 漫游，但它无法让 NPC 遵循日程表、对玩家做出反应，或者在桌前坐下。今天，我们来搭建真正能实现这些的架构。 第 3.2 集将第 3.1 集中的漫游 Timer 替换为一个完整的状态机（State Machine）——每种行为都独立存放在自己的 GDScript 文件中，行为之间的切换被简化为一个返回值。没有新节点，没有新信号，纯粹的架构设计。而它将成为本系列后续所有 NPC 行为的基石。 在本集结束时，添加一个新状态就意味着添加一个新文件。NpcBase 从此再也不需要修改。 在本期教程中，你将学到： 状态设计模式（State Pattern）：了解为什么一旦行为变得复杂，模块化的状态文件就远胜于一个巨大的 match 代码块。 RefCounted vs Node：为什么状态对象完全不应该成为场景树的成员，以及自动内存管理为你带来了什么好处。 三方法契约：enter()、exit()、update()——了解为什么 NpcBase 只需要知道契约本身，而永远不需要了解具体行为。 update() 返回值模式：返回 null 意味着保持当前状态，返回一个新的 NpcState 实例意味着转换。转换逻辑存在于"知道自己何时该离开"的那个状态内部。 无类型 npc 参数与 @warning_ignore_start("untyped_declaration")：解决 NpcState 与 NpcBase 之间的循环依赖问题，这与第 1.3 集中使用的是同一个工具。 Delta 累加替代 Timer 节点：用一个浮点型 _elapsed 变量在状态内部完全取代场景树中的 Timer。 NpcTravelState 与 on_arrive 链式调用：为第 3.3 集的每日日程表奠定基础——走到目的地，然后转换到接下来要执行的任何行为。 call_deferred 的执行顺序：为什么 _set_initial_target() 必须在 _start_state_machine() 之前运行，以及颠倒顺序会导致什么崩溃。 npc_state_changed 信号：每次状态转换都会广播到 GameEvents，任何未来的系统都可以监听，而 NpcBase 完全不需要知道它们的存在。

resources.description:
Basic Movement & Key Presses
What is Pygame?
Pygame is a third party module designed for creating 2D games with python. It has very simple and intuitive syntax that can allows us to create powerful games quickly. Pygame uses surfaces for drawing. This means whenever we want to draw something to the screen it must be converted to a surface. There are many methods and functions within pygame that can do this easily for us.
Installing Pygame
Installing pygame can be as easy as:
Opening your command prompt Typing pip install pygame
However, in many cases this will not work. Below are guides for installing pygame on both windows and mac.
Windows: How to Install Pygame on Windows
Mac OS: How to Install Pygame on Mac
Linux: refer to the Mac OS Guide.
Creating a Window
After we import pygame it is a good idea to initialize it, like so:
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()
```
Once we've done that we need to setup a windows that will represent our game.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500, 500))
# This line creates a window of 500 width, 500 height
```
Now when we run the program we get something that looks like this.
This is great but we'd like to give our game a more creative name than "pygame window". To do this we can can type the following.
```python
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")
```
That's better!
Moving a Character
We are going to start by defining a few variables to represent our character.
x = 50 y = 50 width = 40 height = 60 vel = 5
Now we are going to setup our Main-loop or game-loop. All games have some sort of loop that executes constantly. This loop is responsible for tasks such as checking for events (such as keyboard events or collision), moving objects, updating the display and eventually ending the game. In our game we will use a while loop.
Inside the loop we will implement a time delay so we can control the speed of the game. We will also start by checking for some specific events.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100) # This will delay the game the given amount of milliseconds. In our casee 0.1 seconds will be the delay

    for event in pygame.event.get():  # This will loop through a list of any keyboard or mouse events.
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT: # Checks if the red button in the corner of the window is clicked
            run = False  # Ends the game loop

pygame.quit()  # If we exit the loop this will execute and close our game
```
Now we can draw a rectangle to the screen to represent our character. We will draw the rectangle in the main loop so that it is constantly redrawn each time we loop.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100)

    for event in pygame.event.get():
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
            run = False

    pygame.draw.rect(win, (255,0,0), (x, y, width, height))  #This takes: window/surface, color, rect 
    pygame.display.update() # This updates the screen so we can see our rectangle

pygame.quit()
```
Now we can start checking for events so that we can move our character.

Tutorial #1
In this tutorial series we will be working to create the famous snake game in python with the module pygame. If you are more interested in a general pygame tutorial series click here
Starter Code
To make our lives a bit easier I've set up the main structure for our game already. We are going to be using two main classes (snake and cube).
Creating our Game Loop
In all games we have a loop called a "main loop" or "game loop". This loop will continuously run until the game is exited. It is mainly responsible for checking for events and calling functions and methods based on those events.
We are going to be coding our game loop inside the main() function. We will declare some variables at the top of the function then move into our while loop which will represent our game loop.
```python
def main(): 
    global width, rows, s
    width = 500  # Width of our screen
    height = 500  # Height of our screen
    rows = 20  # Amount of rows

    win = pygame.display.set_mode((width, height))  # Creates our screen object

    s = snake((255,0,0), (10,10))  # Creates a snake object which we will code later

    clock = pygame.time.Clock() # creating a clock object

    flag = True
    # STARTING MAIN LOOP
    while flag:
        pygame.time.delay(50)  # This will delay the game so it doesn't run too quickly
        clock.tick(10)  # Will ensure our game runs at 10 FPS
        redrawWindow(win)  # This will refresh our screen
```
Updating the Screen
It is usually good practice to do all of our drawing of objects from within one function or method. We will be using the redrawWindow function to update the display. We call this function once a frame from our game loop.
We will be adding more to this function later. However, for now we will simply draw the grid lines.
Drawing the Grid
We are now going to work on drawing the lines to represent the 20x20 grid. We will do this in the drawGrid function.
```python
def drawGrid(w, rows, surface):
    sizeBtwn = w // rows  # Gives us the distance between the lines

    x = 0  # Keeps track of the current x
    y = 0  # Keeps track of the current y
    for l in range(rows):  # We will draw one vertical and one horizontal line each loop
        x = x + sizeBtwn
        y = y + sizeBtwn

        pygame.draw.line(surface, (255,255,255), (x,0),(x,w))
        pygame.draw.line(surface, (255,255,255), (0,y),(w,y))
```
Now when we run the program we can see the grid lines being drawn.
Starting the Snake Class
Our snake object is going to contain a list of cubes which will represent the snake body. We are going to store these cubes in a list called body which will be a class variable. We will also have a class variable called turns.
To start our Snake class we will code the init() method and add the class variables.

Basic Movement & Key Presses
What is Pygame?
Pygame is a third party module designed for creating 2D games with python. It has very simple and intuitive syntax that can allows us to create powerful games quickly. Pygame uses surfaces for drawing. This means whenever we want to draw something to the screen it must be converted to a surface. There are many methods and functions within pygame that can do this easily for us.
Installing Pygame
Installing pygame can be as easy as:
Opening your command prompt Typing pip install pygame
However, in many cases this will not work. Below are guides for installing pygame on both windows and mac.
Windows: How to Install Pygame on Windows
Mac OS: How to Install Pygame on Mac
Linux: refer to the Mac OS Guide.
Creating a Window
After we import pygame it is a good idea to initialize it, like so:
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()
```
Once we've done that we need to setup a windows that will represent our game.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500, 500))
# This line creates a window of 500 width, 500 height
```
Now when we run the program we get something that looks like this.
This is great but we'd like to give our game a more creative name than "pygame window". To do this we can can type the following.
```python
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")
```
That's better!
Moving a Character
We are going to start by defining a few variables to represent our character.
x = 50 y = 50 width = 40 height = 60 vel = 5
Now we are going to setup our Main-loop or game-loop. All games have some sort of loop that executes constantly. This loop is responsible for tasks such as checking for events (such as keyboard events or collision), moving objects, updating the display and eventually ending the game. In our game we will use a while loop.
Inside the loop we will implement a time delay so we can control the speed of the game. We will also start by checking for some specific events.

What is Pygame?
Pygame is a third party module designed for creating 2D games with python. It has very simple and intuitive syntax that can allows us to create powerful games quickly. Pygame uses surfaces for drawing. This means whenever we want to draw something to the screen it must be converted to a surface. There are many methods and functions within pygame that can do this easily for us.
Installing Pygame
Installing pygame can be as easy as:
Opening your command prompt Typing pip install pygame
However, in many cases this will not work. Below are guides for installing pygame on both windows and mac.
Windows: How to Install Pygame on Windows
Mac OS: How to Install Pygame on Mac
Linux: refer to the Mac OS Guide.
Creating a Window
After we import pygame it is a good idea to initialize it, like so:
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()
```
Once we've done that we need to setup a windows that will represent our game.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500, 500))
# This line creates a window of 500 width, 500 height
```
Now when we run the program we get something that looks like this.
This is great but we'd like to give our game a more creative name than "pygame window". To do this we can can type the following.
```python
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")
```
That's better!
Moving a Character
We are going to start by defining a few variables to represent our character.
x = 50 y = 50 width = 40 height = 60 vel = 5
Now we are going to setup our Main-loop or game-loop. All games have some sort of loop that executes constantly. This loop is responsible for tasks such as checking for events (such as keyboard events or collision), moving objects, updating the display and eventually ending the game. In our game we will use a while loop.
Inside the loop we will implement a time delay so we can control the speed of the game. We will also start by checking for some specific events.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100) # This will delay the game the given amount of milliseconds. In our casee 0.1 seconds will be the delay

    for event in pygame.event.get():  # This will loop through a list of any keyboard or mouse events.
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT: # Checks if the red button in the corner of the window is clicked
            run = False  # Ends the game loop

pygame.quit()  # If we exit the loop this will execute and close our game
```
Now we can draw a rectangle to the screen to represent our character. We will draw the rectangle in the main loop so that it is constantly redrawn each time we loop.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100)

    for event in pygame.event.get():
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
            run = False

    pygame.draw.rect(win, (255,0,0), (x, y, width, height))  #This takes: window/surface, color, rect 
    pygame.display.update() # This updates the screen so we can see our rectangle

pygame.quit()
```
Now we can start checking for events so that we can move our character.
Inside the if statements we will change the value of the variables x and y to move the character. This brings me to the coordinate system. In pygame the top left corner of the screen is (0,0) and the bottom right is (width, height). This means to move up we subtract from the y of our character and to move down we add to the y.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100)

    for event in pygame.event.get():
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
            run = False

    keys = pygame.key.get_pressed()

    if keys[pygame.K_LEFT]:
        x -= vel

    if keys[pygame.K_RIGHT]:
        x += vel

    if keys[pygame.K_UP]:
        y -= vel

    if keys[pygame.K_DOWN]:
        y += vel

    pygame.draw.rect(win, (255,0,0), (x, y, width, height))   
    pygame.display.update() 

pygame.quit()
```
Now when we run the program and start moving our rectangle we can still see all of the previous rectangles.
To fix this we simply have to draw over the previous shape before redrawing another one. We can use window.fill(color) to do this.
```python
import pygame
pygame.init()

win = pygame.display.set_mode((500,500))
pygame.display.set_caption("First Game")

x = 50
y = 50
width = 40
height = 60
vel = 5

run = True

while run:
    pygame.time.delay(100)

    for event in pygame.event.get():
        if event.type == pygame.QUIT:
            run = False

    keys = pygame.key.get_pressed()

    if keys[pygame.K_LEFT]:
        x -= vel

    if keys[pygame.K_RIGHT]:
        x += vel

    if keys[pygame.K_UP]:
        y -= vel

    if keys[pygame.K_DOWN]:
        y += vel

    win.fill((0,0,0))  # Fills the screen with black
    pygame.draw.rect(win, (255,0,0), (x, y, width, height))   
    pygame.display.update() 

pygame.quit()
```
And now we can move our character around!

evidence.text: Ep 3.2: 告别 Timer！用状态机让 NPC 真正"思考"，Godot游戏开发-小学教程

一个随机的 Timer 可以让 NPC 漫游，但它无法让 NPC 遵循日程表、对玩家做出反应，或者在桌前坐下。今天，我们来搭建真正能实现这些的架构。 第 3.2 集将第 3.1 集中的漫游 Timer 替换为一个完整的状态机（State Machine）——每种行为都独立存放在自己的 GDScript 文件中，行为之间的切换被简化为一个返回值。没有新节点，没有新信号，纯粹的架构设计。而它将成为本系列后续所有 NPC 行为的基石。 在本集结束时，添加一个新状态就意味着添加一个新文件。NpcBase 从此再也不需要修改。 在本期教程中，你将学到： 状态设计模式（State Pattern）：了解为什么一旦行为变得复杂，模块化的状态文件就远胜于一个巨大的 match 代码块。 RefCounted vs Node：为什么状态对象完全不应该成为场景树的成员，以及自动内存管理为你带来了什么好处。 三方法契约：enter()、exit()、update()——了解为什么 NpcBase 只需要知道契约本身，而永远不需要了解具体行为。 update() 返回值模式：返回 null 意味着保持当前状态，返回一个新的 NpcState 实例意味着转换。转换逻辑存在于"知道自己何时该离开"的那个状态内部。 无类型 npc 参数与 @warning_ignore_start("untyped_declaration")：解决 NpcState 与 NpcBase 之间的循环依赖问题，这与第 1.3 集中使用的是同一个工具。 Delta 累加替代 Timer 节点：用一个浮点型 _elapsed 变量在状态内部完全取代场景树中的 Timer。 NpcTravelState 与 on_arrive 链式调用：为第 3.3 集的每日日程表奠定基础——走到目的地，然后转换到接下来要执行的任何行为。 call_deferred 的执行顺序：为什么 _set_initial_target() 必须在 _start_state_machine() 之前运行，以及颠倒顺序会导致什么崩溃。 npc_state_changed 信号：每次状态转换都会广播到 GameEvents，任何未来的系统都可以监听，而 NpcBase 完全不需要知道它们的存在。
